BMW Launching Major Driver Assistance Upgrade for 3 Series, 7 Series, iX3, iX4, and X5 Range in 2027
19 photos
Photo: BMW
BMW has confirmed a pretty substantial driver assistance upgrade for select models based on the Cluster Architecture and the Neue Klasse platform. Starting in Germany from 2027 with the iX3, iX3, X5, 3 Series, and 7 Series , the latest iteration of the system supports navigation-guided urban assistance.
All of the aforementioned models, including the Neue Klasse-based i3 sedan and upcoming wagon, already have the necessary hardware for urban driver assistance functions. While highway setups have become increasingly capable in the past few years, few automakers offer Level 2 systems that are capable of handling the urban jungle's more dynamic and challenging driving scenarios.
The Level 2 system of these Bimmers can assist with urban lane changes, turning maneuvers, navigating roundabouts, and right-of-way situations. Active route guidance through BMW Maps also needs mentioning, with BMW Maps allowing the subject vehicle to anticipate the next maneuver instead of reacting to lane markings and traffic around it.
Having mentioned that, we must remind ourselves that BMW already offers automated stopping and starting at traffic lights through its City Assistant in certain markets. The new urban-centric functions that will be introduced next year expand that capability, and the company's endgame is pretty clear. More specifically, BMW intends to combine Motorway Assistant with City Assistant into a continuous nav-guided experience.
Nobody should confuse that with the act of handing the keys to the car and checking emails while said car does all the driving itself. The Munich-based manufacturer clearly states the system is a Level 2 affair, meaning that drivers must intervene whenever necessary. That also means the driver must remain attentive to what's happening in front and around the vehicle rather than checking emails or sleeping behind the wheel.
Photo: BMW To ensure the driver remains engaged with the act of driving, BMW Symbiotic Drive enables the assistance system and driver to work together instead of competing for control. Think of it this way: when assistance operates, the driver can still brake, accelerate, and steer according to their respective preferences. The system is programmed to interpret their steering behavior and the direction of their gaze to understand the driver's intentions.
This, in turn, makes us consider a lane-keeping assist scenario. A driver who deliberately moves toward a lane marking should not receive the same intervention from the system as someone who has inadvertently drifted out of their lane. Put otherwise, BMW's next iteration of the Level 2 system includes software that distinguishes between intentional driver inputs and situations that genuinely require assistance.
BMW's Panoramic iDrive setup also plays a role in the grand scheme of things, for Panoramic Vision displays all specific assistance information directly in the driver's field of vision. The central infotainment system, meanwhile, gains a three-dimensional BMW Maps with Driver Assistance view that combines navigation guidance, the vehicle's surroundings, and information about which Level 2 functions currently operate.
Although we do know said functions will drop by over-the-air updates, BMW hasn't disclosed whether customers have to pay separately for every additional capability or whether some functions will be locked within existing assistance packages. Oh, and by the way, regulatory approval currently stands between the Bavarian automaker and the rollout to customer vehicles.
Technical requirements are said to have been met, subject to official confirmation in early 2027. The BMW system has a few competitors out there, starting with Tesla's Assisted Driving (a.k.a. Full Self-Driving outside Europe) and Stuttgart's MB.Drive Assist Pro. Over at Audi, the Volkswagen Group's closest equivalent is called Adaptive Driving Assistant Plus.
